The regimen could become a standard in this setting. CHICAGO — The addition of two agents to standard first-line treatment significantly improved PFS among patients with aggressive B-cell lymphomas, according to results of the randomized phase 3 frontMIND trial. Perspectives from Krish Patel, MD; Tycel Phillips, MD The combination of tafasitamab (Monjuvi, Incyte), lenalidomide and R-CHOP reduced risk for progression or death by 25% compared with R-CHOP alone among patients with newly diagnosed high-risk diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, data presented at ASCO Annual Meeting showed. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. Researchers randomly assigned trial participants to R-CHOP alone (n = 451) or R-CHOP plus tafasitamab and lenalidomide (n = 448), with both regimens administered in six 21-day cycles. PFS served as the primary endpoint. EFS and OS served as key secondary endpoints. ‘Good chance’ for cure Median follow-up reached 35.2 months. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). An interim OS analysis showed no statistically significant difference between the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (HR = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.63-1.14), though higher rates of 2-year OS (84.1% vs. 80.5%) and 3-year OS (81.1% vs. 77.8%) with the experimental regimen suggest what researchers described as a trend toward improved survival. “We are seeing a numerical difference of [4 percentage points] so, because the curves are not superimposable, I am cautiously optimistic that over time this might translate into an overall survival benefit,” Lenz said. ‘Manageable’ toxicities The most common adverse events in both treatment groups included cytopenias and infectious events. Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). A higher percentage of patients assigned the experimental regimen experienced grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (86.7% vs. 76.1%). More patients who received tafasitamab and lenalidomide discontinued any part of their treatment (25.7% vs. 17.9%). A comparable percentage of patients in each group discontinued treatment entirely due to adverse events (5.2% vs. 5.4%). Fewer deaths occurred in the experimental group (18.5% vs. 21.7%). Median relative dose intensities of R-CHOP remained high and consistent between groups across all six treatment cycles. “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.” Evolving treatment landscape The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment. The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting. Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment. The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out. “Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.” For more information: Georg Lenz, MD, can be reached at georg.lenz@ukmuenster.de. Unfortunately, it has been difficult to advance on that paradigm, and frontMIND represents only the second phase 3 study to meet its primary endpoint in the last 2 decades. This is an important finding given the consistency of the primary endpoint in subgroups, which is something that has not been found in previous trials. Importantly, PFS is expected to lead to improvement in curative outcomes for these patients, and it is encouraging to see that the delivery of the curative therapy R-CHOP was not compromised by the addition of two new agents. This study tells us that adding multiple-antigen targeting in the front line can lead to an improvement in meaningful clinical efficacy outcomes for our patients. In terms of how long we will use this regimen, Dr. Lenz pointed out the coming trials of frontline bispecifics. Another key question as the frontMIND trial matures is, for those patients who are not cured by the combination of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP, can we still use other CD19-directed therapies as second-line treatment — or even third-line or later — to lead to curative outcomes? Perspective Back to Top Tycel Phillips, MD Tycel Phillips, MD Improving response and curability remains paramount for management of patients with first-line DLBCL, despite improvement of salvage options. The POLARIX study was the first positive phase 3 study, but this trial could be classified more as a double than a home run given that, with long-term follow up, there is no survival benefit and the regimen failed to show any difference vs. R-CHOP in patients with a germinal center subtype of DLBCL. This has led to some hesitation with full implementation of this regimen for all patients. The next foray into this space is the phase 3 frontMIND study, which compares tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP to R-CHOP. The study met its primary endpoint of PFS, but similar to POLARIX, this regimen has not demonstrated a survival benefit at this time. A feather in the cap of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP is the efficacy of the regimen does not appear dependent on cell of origin based on reported data, but judgment is held until the full analysis is available. If we are to assume based on the preliminary data that now we will have access to another treatment regimen, then the next question is whether this is a regimen for all or just select patients. Before we consider this, there a few facts about this regimen that must be considered. First, this regimen is more cumbersome and carries a higher toxicity burden than R-CHOP or polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP, given the inclusion of lenalidomide (cost and adverse events) and tafasitamab (time, due to the weekly infusion schedule). Excluding this, there are still some issues with generalized use of the regimen. The easy answer is, despite the positive results, the study changes nothing for those with low-risk disease (IPI ≤2), who were not included in the study population. The more complicated discussion will be those with an IPI higher than 2. Without having more granular details, the results of the frontMIND study are unlikely to change management for those with nongerminal center B-cell (GCB)/activated B cell subtype DLBCL given the efficacy noted with polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP in this space, coupled with the convenience of this regimen vs. tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP. On the other hand, the frontMIND regimen based on the reported results could be considered the new standard for those with GCB DLBCL and IPI of 3 to 5, excluding those for whom the addition of lenalidomide would be contraindicated. In truth, given the cost — in terms of time, money and toxicity — more details regarding response are needed before fully anointing this regimen as a wholesale replacement for R-CHOP, even for those with germinal center disease. Additionally, data on response for those with high-grade B cell lymphoma and/or double hit lymphoma is pending and would add layers to this discussion given the current utilization of R-DA-EPOCH for these patients vs. R-CHOP. In summary, the early results of the frontMIND study indicate a positive response for the addition of tafasitamab, lenalidomide and rituximab to a CHOP backbone. Without more clarity, this study is likely to provide an impact for a subset of patients with first-line DLBCL vs. completely upending the current treatment paradigm. Data derived from Lenz G, et al. Abstract LBA7000. Presented at: ASCO Annual Meeting; May 29-June 2, 2026; Chicago. The findings — which showed consistent benefit across subgroups defined by clinical and molecular characteristics — will support an application seeking regulatory approval of the regimen in this setting. Georg Lenz “I believe this has a very good chance of being adopted as a standard of care for these high-risk patients,” Georg Lenz, MD , director of the department of hematology and oncology at University Hospital Münster in Germany, told Healio. “The improvement is statistically significant but, to me, it is also clinically meaningful. If you prevent relapse, you prevent the need for subsequent therapies, which is highly relevant for patients — particularly in the high-risk spectrum of disease, where novel therapies are urgently needed.” An unmet need Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma subtype, accounting for more than one-third of cases. R-CHOP chemotherapy — which consists of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab (Rituxan; Genentech, Biogen) plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone — has been a standard first-line treatment for more than 2 decades. However, approximately 40% of patients with DLBCL are not cured with this regimen, underscoring a need for more effective treatments — particularly for people with high-risk disease. “We clearly need better therapies upfront because, if a patient relapses after failing frontline therapy, the chances we will be able to cure that patient are lower than the chances the patient will die of aggressive lymphoma,” Lenz said. Tafasitamab, an anti-CD19 antibody, is approved in the United States in combination with lenalidomide for adults with relapsed or refractory DLBCL who are not eligible for autologous stem cell transplant. The phase 1b First-MIND study showed encouraging efficacy and safety with tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP as treatment of newly diagnosed DLBCL. Lenz and colleagues conducted the double-blind, placebo-controlled frontMIND trial to evaluate the combination as first-line treatment for patients with high-intermediate or high-risk aggressive B-cell lymphomas. The international trial included 899 adults (median age, 65 years; range, 18-80) with previously untreated DLBCL or high-grade B-cell lymphoma, which is less common but more aggressive than DLBCL. All patients — recruited from North America, South America, Asia and Europe — had high-risk disease per International Prognostic Index criteria. They also had ECOG performance status of 0 to 2 and at least one measurable PET-positive lesion per local assessment. The primary endpoint analysis showed a 25% reduction in risk for disease progression or death among patients assigned tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59-0.96). The risk reduction reached 32% among trial participants (n = 773) whose diagnosis had been centrally confirmed. The PFS benefit persisted across all predefined subgroups, including patients grouped by major molecular subtypes based on cell of origin. Median PFS had not been reached, but a higher percentage of patients who received the experimental regimen remained progression free at 2 years (71.1% vs. 62.9%) and 3 years (67.3% vs. 60.7%). “Hematologists and oncologists are reluctant to use the word ‘cure,’ but having a relapse of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after 2 years is rather rare,” Lenz said. “With the follow-up we have, the patients who are still in remission have quite a good chance of being cured.” Secondary endpoint analyses showed improved EFS with the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide to R-CHOP (HR = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.64-0.97), with higher EFS rates in that group at 2 years (65% vs. 56.7%) and 3 years (61.2% vs. 54.8%). Comparable rates of any-grade treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in the experimental and R-CHOP alone groups (98.6% vs. 97.1%). “The toxicities overall were manageable,” Lenz said. “It is important to note that the addition of tafasitamab and lenalidomide did not compromise the delivery of the R-CHOP backbone, which obviously is important to cure patients.”
Evolving treatment landscape
The frontMIND trial is only the second randomized phase 3 trial evaluating first-line treatment approaches for DLBCL over the past 20 years to demonstrate improvement in its primary efficacy outcome compared with standard treatment.
The POLARIX trial, results of which were published in The New England Journal of Medicine , showed the antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) plus R-CHP — a modified R-CHOP regimen that does not include vincristine — reduced risk for progression, relapse or death compared with R-CHOP for patients with previously untreated intermediate-risk or high-risk DLBCL. Polatuzumab vedotin plus R-CHP is approved in the U.S. in that setting.
The New England Journal of Medicine
Bispecific antibodies have demonstrated activity in the relapsed/refractory setting. Two randomized phase 3 trials designed to evaluate those types of therapies for untreated patients have completed enrollment.
The SKYGLO trial will evaluate the addition of glofitamab (Columvi, Genentech) to polatuzumab vedotin and R-CHP as frontline treatment for CD20-positive large B-cell lymphoma. The EPCORE DLBCL-2 trial will assess the addition of subcutaneous epcoritamab (Epkinly; Genmab, AbbVie) to R-CHOP for newly diagnosed, high-risk DLBCL.
epcoritamab
The results of those trials likely will influence the role that tafasitamab, lenalidomide and R-CHOP regimen has in the lymphoma treatment armamentarium, Lenz said.
“The results of frontMIND are very promising. I assume this regimen will get regulatory approval and I think it will be used,” Lenz said. “For how long? I think that depends on results of the other trials. They are fully recruited, but it will take time for them to read out.
“Given the efficacy of bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory disease, I think one can be optimistic that these studies will also be positive,” Lenz added. “That could further change the treatment landscape. It’s fantastic, after 20 years of not having much movement, we could be able to offer patients multiple different therapeutic options.”

Skip to content Suggested Topics: Home Best in Biotech Eight oncology deals in 2026 spotlight where industry leaders are betting big Photo credits: Cytonn Photography (Unsplash) Newsletter Signup - Under Article / In Page " * " indicates required fields Biotech partnerships play a critical role in driving innovation through the sharing of knowledge, expertise, and resources, and are particularly important in bridging the gap between early-stage research and commercial development. As oncology consistently dominates biotech deal-making activity , accounting for a significant portion of both deal volume and value, large pharmaceutical companies are continuously seeking to bolster their own pipelines with promising cancer assets developed by promising biotech innovators. In this article, we look at eight of the biggest oncology deals that have been made so far in 2026. Table of contents Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics AbbVie and RemeGen BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Roche and C4 Therapeutics Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS. The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs. Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion. Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines. The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.” The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The agreement also grants Eli Lilly an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the programs worldwide outside Greater China, while Innovent retains rights in Greater China. Suggested Articles The ABC of biotech partnerships T cell engagers: A promising, fast-growing field for cancer and autoimmune disease treatments Are molecular glues the key to undruggable targets? The radiopharmaceutical revolution: From diagnosis to treatment, oncology and beyond Eight biotech companies spearheading the antibody drug conjugate new wave The financial terms of the deal included a $350 million upfront payment for Innovent, with the company also eligible to receive up to approximately $8.5 billion in development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments. AbbVie and RemeGen Back to Top At the start of the year, AbbVie entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with RemeGen for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of RC148, a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-targeted bispecific antibody, which is currently being developed by RemeGen as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across multiple advanced solid tumors. PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs. In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer. Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory. BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis. PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs. In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer. Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory. BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis. Through its “three-in-one” synergistic mechanism of action, the asset is expected to enhance therapeutic efficacy, achieve tumor-specific drug distribution, and reduce treatment-related adverse effects. Positive preclinical results for it were presented at the 2025 Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) in Chicago, in the U.S. Under the agreement, Huahui Health received an upfront payment of $20 million. Additionally, the Chinese biotech is entitled to receive an additional $100 million option exercise payment and is eligible to receive up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Back to Top February 2026 saw Japanese big pharma Astellas enter into a global strategic collaboration with Vir Biotechnology to advance VIR-5500, a PRO-XTEN dual-masked CD3 T-cell engager targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) for the treatment of prostate cancer. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership. Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%. VIR-5500 is currently in phase 1 of development for people with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. The candidate combines a bispecific PSMA and CD3-binding T-cell engager with the PRO-XTEN masking technology, which is designed to keep the T-cell engagers masked (or inactive) until they reach the tumor microenvironment, reducing off-target effects and improving the therapeutic index. The financial terms of the agreement stated that Vir Biotechnology would receive $335 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments, would split U.S. profit/loss equally with Astellas (50/50), and would be eligible to receive up to an additional $1.37 billion in development, regulatory, and sales milestones, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on ex-U.S. net sales. Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Back to Top In February, Gilead Sciences stepped deeper into synthetic lethality by licensing a methionine adenosyltransferase 2a (MAT2A) inhibitor from China-based Genhouse Bio. At the time of the deal, the asset, dubbed GH31, was being developed by Genhouse for various tumor types and had already been given the green light from Chinese and U.S. regulators to enter clinical trials. Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales. This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die. These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise. Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer. Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization. Meanwhile, the financial terms of the oncology deal stated that C4T would receive a $20 million upfront payment and, should Roche exercise its option for a third target, C4T would receive an additional payment. C4T is also eligible to receive more than $1 billion in discovery, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments and is entitled to tiered royalties on future sales, subject to reductions under certain circumstances as described in the agreement. As oncology consistently dominates biotech deal-making activity , accounting for a significant portion of both deal volume and value, large pharmaceutical companies are continuously seeking to bolster their own pipelines with promising cancer assets developed by promising biotech innovators. In this article, we look at eight of the biggest oncology deals that have been made so far in 2026. Table of contents Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics AbbVie and RemeGen BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Roche and C4 Therapeutics Bristol Myers Squibb and Hengrui Pharma Back to Top In May, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) announced an extensive strategic collaboration with Chinese biotech company Hengrui Pharma to advance a portfolio of 13 early-stage programs in oncology, hematology, and immunology, with the goal of accelerating discovery and development of innovative medicines for the benefit of patients worldwide. The agreement includes four oncology/hematology assets from Hengrui, four immunology assets from BMS, and five innovative assets to be discovered and developed by both companies, which will leverage Hengrui’s discovery engine and platform technologies across several modalities. Hengrui also has the option to co-develop select assets and the potential to conduct certain commercialization activities globally with BMS. The terms also stated that BMS obtains exclusive worldwide rights to the Hengrui‑originated assets everywhere outside the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong SAR, and Macau SAR, while Hengrui obtains exclusive rights to the BMS‑originated assets within these territories. Additionally, Hengrui is responsible for early clinical development to accelerate clinical proof of concept for these programs. Financially, the deal was a big one, with a total deal value of up to approximately $15.2 billion. Pfizer and Innovent Biologics Back to Top In another extensive deal in May, worth up to $10.5 billion, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics entered into a strategic global licensing and collaboration agreement for the research and development of 12 promising breakthrough early-stage and de novo cancer medicines. The agreement specifically includes licensing, co-development, and co-commercialization opportunities across a diverse portfolio of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) with novel differentiated payloads and multi-specific antibodies with differentiated “immune-engaging features and unique designs.” The 12 programs involved in the oncology deal include eight Innovent-originated early-stage programs and four Pfizer-proposed discovery programs, with the companies co-developing and sharing costs for select programs as they advance them through clinical development. Additionally, according to the agreement, Innovent is to conduct the development of these programs through phase 1, after which Pfizer will lead future global development. Eli Lilly and Innovent Biologics Back to Top The Pfizer collaboration was not the only big oncology deal for Innovent Biologics so far this year; the Chinese biotech also announced a strategic collaboration with long-standing partner Eli Lilly in February to advance novel medicines in oncology and immunology, marking the seventh collaboration between the two companies. The agreement stated that the companies would leverage their “complementary strengths” to accelerate global development of novel medicines. Drawing on its antibody technology platforms and efficient clinical execution, Innovent will lead the development of programs from concept through to clinical proof-of-concept (phase 2 clinical trial completion) in China. The agreement also grants Eli Lilly an exclusive license to develop and commercialize the programs worldwide outside Greater China, while Innovent retains rights in Greater China. The financial terms of the deal included a $350 million upfront payment for Innovent, with the company also eligible to receive up to approximately $8.5 billion in development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments.
AbbVie and RemeGen Back to Top
At the start of the year, AbbVie entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with RemeGen for the development, manufacturing, and commercialization of RC148, a programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-targeted bispecific antibody, which is currently being developed by RemeGen as a monotherapy and in combination regimens across multiple advanced solid tumors.
PD-1/VEGF-targeted bispecific antibodies are a hot area right now in biotech and represent a new class of cancer therapies that aim to help the immune system fight tumors more effectively and potentially overcome tumor resistance mechanisms by blocking both PD-1 and VEGF simultaneously. Additionally, given their potential to modulate both immune suppression and to foster a favorable tumor microenvironment for ADC activity, this class of therapies is also being explored in combination with ADCs.
In early clinical studies, RC148 has shown initial favorable antitumor activity in combination with an ADC. This means that the candidate could offer AbbVie the option to explore combination regimens with its own ADCs, such as investigational telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A), across multiple solid tumors with high unmet need, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer.
Under the terms of the agreement, AbbVie receives exclusive rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize RC148 outside of the Greater China territory. Meanwhile, financially, RemeGen received an upfront payment of $650 million and is also eligible to receive up to $4.95 billion in aggregate development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on net sales outside the Greater China territory.
BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health Back to Top
In April, BeOne Medicines and Huahui Health formed an oncology deal in which BeOne Medicines was granted an exclusive option covering the worldwide development, manufacturing, and commercialization of HH160, a trispecific antibody that simultaneously targets PD-1, CTLA-4, and VEGF-A – three clinically validated targets in cancer immunotherapy and anti-angiogenesis.
formed
trispecific antibody
Through its “three-in-one” synergistic mechanism of action, the asset is expected to enhance therapeutic efficacy, achieve tumor-specific drug distribution, and reduce treatment-related adverse effects. Positive preclinical results for it were presented at the 2025 Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) in Chicago, in the U.S.
Under the agreement, Huahui Health received an upfront payment of $20 million. Additionally, the Chinese biotech is entitled to receive an additional $100 million option exercise payment and is eligible to receive up to $1.9 billion in milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties on net sales.
Astellas and Vir Biotechnology Back to Top
February 2026 saw Japanese big pharma Astellas enter into a global strategic collaboration with Vir Biotechnology to advance VIR-5500, a PRO-XTEN dual-masked CD3 T-cell engager targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) for the treatment of prostate cancer. The deal aims to accelerate the development of Vir Biotechnology’s asset and further strengthen Astellas’ oncology pipeline and prostate cancer leadership.
enter into
T-cell engager
Despite recent advances in treatment, prostate cancer, especially metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, remains an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat; metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has a 5-year survival rate of approximately 30%.
survival rate
VIR-5500 is currently in phase 1 of development for people with advanced, metastatic prostate cancer. The candidate combines a bispecific PSMA and CD3-binding T-cell engager with the PRO-XTEN masking technology, which is designed to keep the T-cell engagers masked (or inactive) until they reach the tumor microenvironment, reducing off-target effects and improving the therapeutic index.
The financial terms of the agreement stated that Vir Biotechnology would receive $335 million in upfront and near-term milestone payments, would split U.S. profit/loss equally with Astellas (50/50), and would be eligible to receive up to an additional $1.37 billion in development, regulatory, and sales milestones, along with tiered, double-digit royalties on ex-U.S. net sales.
Gilead Sciences and Genhouse Bio Back to Top
In February, Gilead Sciences stepped deeper into synthetic lethality by licensing a methionine adenosyltransferase 2a (MAT2A) inhibitor from China-based Genhouse Bio. At the time of the deal, the asset, dubbed GH31, was being developed by Genhouse for various tumor types and had already been given the green light from Chinese and U.S. regulators to enter clinical trials.
licensing
Under the agreement, Genhouse received more than $80 million upfront and is eligible to receive up to $1.45 billion in milestone payments, as well as royalties based on tiered double-digit percentages on net sales.
This was Gilead’s second synthetic lethal therapy deal in a short space of time after it also acquired Repare Therapeutics’ polymerase theta (Polθ) ATPase inhibitor, RP-3467, in December 2025. Synthetic lethality occurs when mutations in two genes together result in cell death, but a mutation in either gene alone does not. Cancer cells that only have one mutated gene in a specific pair of genes can depend on the normal partner gene for survival. Therefore, interfering with the function of the normal partner gene may cause cancer cells to die.
acquired
These deals show how oncology has now become the central pillar of Gilead’s pipeline strategy as it moves beyond its HIV franchise.
Gilead’s pipeline strategy
Roche and C4 Therapeutics Back to Top
In April, Roche and C4 Therapeutics (C4T) expanded their long-term partnership, entering into a new collaboration focused on advancing research in the emerging degrader-antibody conjugate modality , which essentially combines ADCs and targeted protein degradation to leverage both the specificity and catalytic efficiency of degraders with the delivery capabilities of ADCs to treat cancer.
entering into
degrader-antibody conjugate modality
Under their joint research plan, Roche and C4T are collaborating on two programs to develop degrader-antibody conjugates against undisclosed oncology targets exclusive to the collaboration. C4T will use its TORPEDO platform to design degrader payload candidates, while Roche will select and design the antibody, as well as conjugate the antibody to the degrader payload. The big pharma will also be responsible for advancing degrader-antibody conjugate candidates through preclinical and clinical development, as well as commercialization.
Meanwhile, the financial terms of the oncology deal stated that C4T would receive a $20 million upfront payment and, should Roche exercise its option for a third target, C4T would receive an additional payment. C4T is also eligible to receive more than $1 billion in discovery, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments and is entitled to tiered royalties on future sales, subject to reductions under certain circumstances as described in the agreement.

articles.title: WuXi Biologics gets South Korean GMP certification for bispecific antibody
articles.text:
Industry News WuXi Biologics gets South Korean GMP certification for bispecific antibody The certification enables end-to-end commercial manufacturing across drug substance, fill-finish, and packaging for complex biologics targeting oncology indications. April 24, 2026 2 min read WuXi Biologics, a global contract research, development, and manufacturing organization (CRDMO), announced that three manufacturing facilities in Wuxi, China, have received Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) certification from South Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety, enabling commercial manufacturing of a bispecific antibody for biliary tract cancer. The certification covers the company’s Drug Substance Facility 5, Drug Product Facility 2, and Drug Product Packaging Center, supporting integrated capabilities from drug substance manufacturing through fill-finish and packaging. The approval follows a five-day inspection with no critical or major findings. According to the company , the certified facilities are part of its global GMP network and provide end-to-end manufacturing services designed to support commercial-scale production of complex biologics. The integrated setup is intended to streamline supply and improve operational efficiency for biologics programs targeting global markets. WuXi Biologics said the certification strengthens its ability to support customers in South Korea and the broader Asia-Pacific region, particularly for advanced modalities such as bispecific antibodies. The development aligns with the company’s broader strategy to expand its integrated CRDMO model , which combines research, development and manufacturing capabilities to improve speed, flexibility and consistency across biologics programs. The company has reported growing demand for complex modalities, including bispecific and multispecific antibodies, within its pipeline. April 29, 2026 2 min read shutterstock_2461469693 CellProthera, a biotechnology company headquartered in Mulhouse, France, has entered a collaboration with Quintessence Biotech to optimize cell therapy manufacturing processes ahead of clinical trials for ischemic stroke. The partnership will integrate Quintessence Biotech’s flotation-based cell sorting platform into CellProthera’s manufacturing workflow for its CD34+ cell therapy candidate, with the goal of improving cell yield, preserving stem cell phenotype and enhancing product quality, the company said. The technology is designed to simplify cell sorting by eliminating the need for magnetic separation systems and specialized consumables, while enabling integration into existing cell culture environments, according to the announcement. CellProthera said the collaboration supports its broader manufacturing strategy as it prepares for Phase 3 production of its lead therapy for acute myocardial infarction, while exploring expansion into stroke indications that may require higher cell doses. Further testing will focus on adapting the platform to specific process requirements and scaling manufacturing performance. The agreement builds on CellProthera’s ongoing efforts to establish late-stage manufacturing capabilities. In 2025, the company selected CellforCURE by Seqens to support Phase 3 GMP manufacturing of its CD34+ therapy, including technology transfer and clinical batch production for a planned late-stage trial. The development aligns with the company’s broader strategy to expand its integrated CRDMO model , which combines research, development and manufacturing capabilities to improve speed, flexibility and consistency across biologics programs. The company has reported growing demand for complex modalities, including bispecific and multispecific antibodies, within its pipeline. Armin Spura, CEO of BioDuro, said in a statement that combining BioDuro’s integrated discovery and development capabilities with CTI’s GLP toxicology and bioanalytical expertise is intended to help clients advance innovative programs with greater speed and efficiency. Tony Liu, general manager of CTI Biotechnology, said in a statement the collaboration will provide clients worldwide with a more complete and efficient integrated preclinical development solution. The agreement builds on BioDuro’s recent efforts to expand its development and manufacturing network. Last month, the company announced a joint venture in Taiwan to increase API manufacturing capacity , integrating early-stage development capabilities with commercial-scale GMP production to support clinical through commercial supply. April 24, 2026 2 min read CordenPharma CordenPharma, a contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) headquartered in Basel, Switzerland, announced the successful completion of regulatory inspections by Brazil’s ANVISA and South Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) at its Plankstadt, Germany facility. The ANVISA inspection, which focused on the manufacture of a highly potent drug product, concluded ahead of its planned five-day schedule and included a review of manufacturing areas, laboratories, warehouse operations and supporting technical functions, the company said. The MFDS inspection, conducted one week later, also spanned five days and evaluated end-to-end GMP systems for a first-in-class highly potent drug product, including engineering, documentation and operational compliance, according to the CDMO. CordenPharma said both inspections resulted in zero observations, confirming the site’s GMP framework and its ability to manage complex, highly potent manufacturing processes. The company said the outcome supports its containment strategies and operational controls for handling highly potent compounds. The Plankstadt facility’s inspection results come as the company continues to expand its global manufacturing and development footprint. Last month, CordenPharma announced an expansion of its peptide development capabilities in Boulder, Colorado, adding laboratory space to support process development and analytical services alongside its existing peptide API manufacturing operations. The company said the expanded capabilities are intended to improve alignment between development and manufacturing activities and support growing outsourcing demand across its global network. Industry News Ori Biotech, AdAlta, Cell Therapies team on automated cell therapy platform The teaming aims to improve scalability, consistency, and speed for CAR-T and other cell therapy manufacturing in the Asia-Pacific region. April 23, 2026 2 min read Ori Biotech AdAlta, a Melbourne, Australia-based biotechnology company, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Ori Biotech, headquartered in London, and Cell Therapies to deploy Ori Biotech’s automated IRO cell therapy manufacturing platform across the  Asia-Pacific region. According to the announcement, the collaboration aims to address key manufacturing challenges in CAR-T and other cell therapies, including high costs, limited scalability and inconsistent production outcomes. Ori’s IRO platform is reportedly designed to automate and standardize critical steps in cell therapy manufacturing, with targets of 10-50x higher throughput, shorter production timelines, and potential cost reductions of 30-50%. The companies said the platform will be deployed at Cell Therapies for process development and clinical manufacturing, while also supporting optimization of AdAlta’s manufacturing processes to improve scalability and reduce costs. The agreement also seeks to expand manufacturing capacity for additional developers across preclinical, clinical, and commercial programs. AdAlta said the collaboration supports its strategy to deliver scalable and cost-effective cell therapies for solid tumors to global markets, including programs that may benefit from more advanced manufacturing capabilities. Ori’s IRO platform has been used in multiple manufacturing processes and has received an Advanced Manufacturing Technology designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which is intended to support adoption of technologies that improve manufacturing reliability and scalability. The agreement builds on Ori Biotech’s broader efforts to expand adoption of automated manufacturing. Late last year , the company announced a collaboration with Seattle Children’s Research Institute to evaluate the IRO platform’s ability to improve scalability and consistency in cell and gene therapy development. April 23, 2026 2 min read
April 23, 2026
Ori Biotech
AdAlta, a Melbourne, Australia-based biotechnology company, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Ori Biotech, headquartered in London, and Cell Therapies to deploy Ori Biotech’s automated IRO cell therapy manufacturing platform across the  Asia-Pacific region. According to the announcement, the collaboration aims to address key manufacturing challenges in CAR-T and other cell therapies, including high costs, limited scalability and inconsistent production outcomes. Ori’s IRO platform is reportedly designed to automate and standardize critical steps in cell therapy manufacturing, with targets of 10-50x higher throughput, shorter production timelines, and potential cost reductions of 30-50%. The companies said the platform will be deployed at Cell Therapies for process development and clinical manufacturing, while also supporting optimization of AdAlta’s manufacturing processes to improve scalability and reduce costs. The agreement also seeks to expand manufacturing capacity for additional developers across preclinical, clinical, and commercial programs. AdAlta said the collaboration supports its strategy to deliver scalable and cost-effective cell therapies for solid tumors to global markets, including programs that may benefit from more advanced manufacturing capabilities. Ori’s IRO platform has been used in multiple manufacturing processes and has received an Advanced Manufacturing Technology designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which is intended to support adoption of technologies that improve manufacturing reliability and scalability. The agreement builds on Ori Biotech’s broader efforts to expand adoption of automated manufacturing. Late last year , the company announced a collaboration with Seattle Children’s Research Institute to evaluate the IRO platform’s ability to improve scalability and consistency in cell and gene therapy development. articles.title: Akeso and Summit's ivonescimab extends survival in squamous cell lung cancer
articles.text:

STAT Plus Biotech Akeso and Summit’s ivonescimab extends survival in squamous cell lung cancer ‘Two drugs in one’ candidate, developed in China, is a highlight at ASCO Manage alerts for this article Email this article Share this article By Matthew Herper May 31, 2026 Senior Writer, Medicine, Editorial Director of Events Matthew Herper matthew.herper@statnews.com Matthew Herper covers medical innovation — both its promise and its perils. Get email alerts for Matthew Herper Signed up for email alerts Remove email alerts Subscribe or log in to STAT+ to unlock email alerts CHICAGO — Ivonescimab, a drug that combines the activity of two of the best-selling cancer medicines, reduced the risk of death in patients with squamous non-small cell lung cancer by 34% compared to a standard treatment in a clinical trial conducted entirely in China by the drug’s developer, Akeso, according to data presented Sunday. The result, oncologists say, exceeded their expectations, and it appears it could generate optimism for the drug, which is being developed outside China by Summit Therapeutics. But the data also are likely to fuel debate on issues like the role of China in drug development and the future of cancer treatments. The results were presented here at the annual meeting of the American Society of Clinical Oncology and are being published simultaneously in The Lancet . Advertisement Robert Duggan, Summit’s co-CEO and chairman, said that the data mean the company has “a very valuable business with a very valuable product that is in its early stages.” Akeso had no comment for this story. articles.title: How to Decode the Chemical Fingerprints of PFAS
articles.text:
Skip to main content Article How to Decode the Chemical Fingerprints of PFAS By looking for clues “forever chemicals” leave behind in people’s blood, researchers hope to understand how PFAS affect the human body. Written by Carrie McDonough, PhD Carrie McDonough, PhD Carrie McDonough, PhD is an Associate Professor of Chemistry at Carnegie Mellon University. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and The Conversation The Conversation The Conversation is a nonprofit, independent news organization dedicated to unlocking the knowledge of experts for the public good. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 6, 2026 | 7 min read Save for Later PFAS compounds are found in nonstick cookware, food packaging, cosmetics, textiles, and even toilet paper. Image credit: © iStock.com, Love Employee PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share V irtually every living thing on Earth, from Patagonian penguins to newborn human babies, has been touched by the synthetic chemicals known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS . In fact, you would be hard pressed to find a sample of human blood, tissue or breast milk without detectable levels of at least one type of PFAS. 1,2 Making matters worse, researchers are continually uncovering links between human exposure to PFAS and poor health outcomes, including a weakened immune system, a heightened risk of kidney and testicular cancer, and pregnancy complications, including preeclampsia and reduced birth weight. 3,4 The levels of some PFAS considered safe in US drinking water are decreasing. 5 Despite this, The Trump administration is in the process of revoking and possibly rewriting proposed regulations for all but PFOA and PFOS, two of the most commonly used PFAS until the early 2000s. US maximum contaminant level goals for PFOA and PFOS are 0 parts per trillion – meaning there are no levels the US Environmental Protection Agency considers safe. Meanwhile, thousands of PFAS have not been studied and have no regulation or oversight. 6 In many cases, there is no monitoring data on their presence in consumer products, water and food. As an expert in chemical pollution , I have studied a wide range of synthetic and natural chemicals that can have harmful health effects for humans and wildlife. A major focus of my current research is tracing PFAS from their initial source – including consumer products, contaminated food and water, and the air – to their resulting fingerprint in an organism’s blood and tissues. 7 Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Immunology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe By following the journey of how PFAS move into the bodies of living things – including people – scientists like me are working to improve safety recommendations and usage guidelines for these chemicals. First, though, we need to understand how these complex chemical mixtures are transformed as they accumulate in the body. What Are PFAS? PFAS are a large class of organic chemicals – meaning molecules that contain carbon atoms – that have fluorine atoms added to them. This fluorination allows PFAS to aggregate on surfaces in ways that are desirable for many applications. For example, PFAS are used in nonstick cookware, food packaging, cosmetics, textiles and even toilet paper, among many other commercial and industrial products. 8 They’re also heavily used in semiconductor manufacturing and lithium-ion batteries. 9 When PFAS are everywhere, they’re hard to avoid. PFAS are commonly called forever chemicals because of their astonishing persistence – due to the strong chemical bonds between carbon and fluorine, they don’t break down easily. This durability is desirable for manufacturers, as materials made with PFAS can function for a long time without degrading. However, persistence becomes problematic when PFAS leach or evaporate out of products and into the surrounding environment. PFAS can remain in drinking water sources and in sediment for decades to centuries. 10,11 If dissolved in water or released into the air, PFAS can also travel long distances from their point of origin, ending up in remote locations. 12 For example, PFAS initially released from industrial regions can end up in the blood of white sharks in the Atlantic Ocean or in Arctic environments. 13,14 PFAS Fingerprints What happens when PFAS are absorbed and accumulate in the body? When someone is exposed to PFAS, it leaves a unique pattern of chemical contamination – what researchers call a PFAS fingerprint – in their blood. 15 Studying these PFAS fingerprints enables scientists to learn about sources of PFAS exposure and how they differ among people who live in different places, have different jobs and use different products, among other factors. But to be able to use these PFAS fingerprints, researchers first need to understand how specific exposures contribute to someone’s PFAS fingerprint over time. The composition of this fingerprint is different from the mixture of chemicals someone was initially exposed to, as some PFAS accumulate in blood to a greater extent than others. Without understanding how a PFAS mixture is distorted and changed in the body, it’s very difficult to know what sources were major contributors to a person’s lifelong PFAS exposure. For example, firefighters and military service members use aqueous film-forming foams that contain hundreds of poorly studied PFAS. These are soapy, sudsy materials that form a film over fire and starve it of oxygen. They’re commonly used in emergencies, such as airplane crashes, train wrecks, vehicle fires or any other fire involving fuels. The PFAS in firefighting foam are suspected to be significant occupational health hazards. Jim Peaco/Yellowstone Digital Slide Files Many firefighters and first responders who have used these foams are now grappling with serious health problems, including cancer, and many have wondered whether PFAS contributed to their illness. A clearer understanding of the PFAS fingerprint that would be expected in someone’s blood after years of using these foams could help determine whether they are a unique source of the PFAS accumulating in their blood. PFAS in the Body Fingerprints at the scene of a crime are often a major clue leading detectives to the perpetrator. When it comes to identifying sources of PFAS contaminating human bodies, however, researchers like me aren’t always so lucky. For one, PFAS are typically present at low concentrations in the environment but can build up to higher levels in the body . For example, people drinking water containing PFOS will typically have levels 50 to 100 times higher in their blood than were measured in the water. 16 This is because the body’s rate of PFOS uptake exceeds its rate of excretion. But not all PFAS will increase in blood to the same degree. PFAS that are more likely to bind to biological components, such as proteins and fats, will more readily accumulate in the body. 17 As the mixture of chemicals in drinking water, for example, continues to accumulate in the body, these types of more bioaccumulative PFAS, such as PFOS, will make up a higher proportion of the fingerprint than other types. This distortion complicates my and other scientists’ job, since we need to be able to predict how much each PFAS accumulates in the body to estimate how these chemicals will change in the body. Do you know how much and what types of PFAS are in your water? show999/iStock via Getty Images Plus On top of predicting which PFAS will accumulate in the body and which will be excreted, researchers also have to contend with a person’s metabolism, the process by which chemicals – including some PFAS – are biologically transformed by the body. Although the chemical structure of PFAS may change in the body, the resulting chemical is usually still a PFAS: a highly fluorinated molecule. After entering the body, many types of PFAS used in different products can be transformed over days to years, while the highly fluorinated backbone of the molecule remains intact. By these processes, many different PFAS eventually transform into just a few highly persistent PFAS. 18 For example, many distinct PFAS containing a PFOS backbone can ultimately change to PFOS in the body. 19 Once these distinct PFAS have all become the same common chemical, it may be impossible to identify how a person was initially exposed. Protecting Yourself From PFAS Despite all the complexities of PFAS research, researchers are making progress toward better understanding how these thousands of chemicals accumulate and transform in the body. Studying real products that contain complex PFAS mixtures can help researchers get closer to finding biomarkers that can pinpoint a PFAS source in a person’s blood. The most effective way to protect human health would be to cease the use of PFAS entirely in all but the most essential of products. 20 Until then, consumers can look to resources such as those from the Green Science Policy Institute and Environmental Working Group to help them avoid PFAS in products they use. There are also a number of commercial laboratories that offer drinking water and blood testing for some common PFAS. But it’s important to remember that these tests don’t capture the whole picture of your PFAS fingerprint. 21 Scientists like me are still hard at work capturing many more PFAS that have been overlooked. Related Topics Biochemistry , contamination , environmental exposure , Perfluorinated compounds , pollution , Public Health , toxicity Meet the Author Carrie McDonough, PhD Carrie McDonough, PhD is an Associate Professor of Chemistry at Carnegie Mellon University. The McDonough Lab investigates organic pollutants, how they are transformed and transported through the environment from point of origin, where they end up, and their potential impacts on water quality, environmental quality, and human and ecosystem health. We use high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), ion mobility, and other advanced analytical strategies to expand detection and deepen understanding of impacts of organic contaminants that are undiscovered and/or overlooked. Much of our work investigates the identification and prioritization of synthetic organics based on propensity to be available to and accumulative in living things. This requires an understanding of how complex, exposure-relevant mixtures of pollutants interact with and are transformed by biological systems. We develop and evaluate materials that are selective for bioavailable and bioaccumulative chemicals in complex environments to decrease reliance on use of living organisms in risk assessment research. We use our expertise in environmental analytical chemistry and nontarget analysis to develop workflows to assess the environmental and public health risks of novel contaminants and to learn about how environmental processes and novel remediation techniques impact environmentally-relevant mixtures. Our work emphasizes the importance of evaluating not only toxicity, but also bioavailability, bioaccumulation, and biological transformation in environmental risk assessment. The Nutshell A Pavlovian Twist: Mosquitoes Learn to Love DEET Trained mosquitoes learned to associate the smell of the repellent with food and actively sought out DEET-covered skin, offering insight on how best to apply the repellent. Written by RJ Mackenzie RJ Mackenzie Go to The Scientist's LinkedIn Page RJ is a freelance science writer based in Glasgow. He covers biological and biomedical science, with a focus on the complexities and curiosities of the brain and emerging AI technologies. RJ has a Master’s degree in Clinical Neurosciences from the University of Cambridge. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 28, 2026 | 2 min read Save for Later Researchers trained the mosquito Aedes aegypti to become hungry upon smelling DEET insect repellent. Image credit: © iStock.com, Oleg Marchak PDF version Share M osquito-borne diseases kill around one million people every year. One of the few tools available to reliably ward off these blood-sucking insects is the repellent chemical N, N-diethyl-meta-toluamide (DEET). DEET also repels ticks and flies, but some researchers have suggested that it loses its effectiveness after repeated exposure. Now, scientists have taken this idea one step further, showing that mosquitoes can even learn to love the chemical if it is associated with food rewards. 1 In new research published in the Journal of Experimental Biology , these trained mosquitoes actually bit people who were soaked in DEET more than those who wore no repellent at all. Claudio Lazzari , a biologist at the University of Tours and coauthor of the study, said in a statement that DEET likely mimics natural insect repellents released by plants and that the spray remains society’s best hope for repelling the bugs. The new study, he said, could offer hints about how best to apply DEET to minimize the chance of getting bitten. Mosquitoes Get the Munchies Lazzari and his team developed a series of experiments inspired by the foundational behavioral work of physiologist Ivan Pavlov , who trained dogs to associate food with the noise of a bell. While Pavlov recorded how the bell made his dogs drool, the mosquito scientists instead measured how strongly the insects reached for a blood reward by sticking their probosces through a fabric mesh. This jabbing motion was termed the biting attempt response (BAR). Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Newsletter updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe The team offered the mosquitoes blood while pumping air laced with DEET into their test chamber. At first, this put the bugs off their meal. The team then shook things up by offering blood to the insects for 30 seconds and only pumping in DEET for the last 10 seconds. After just three rounds of this sequenced exposure, the smell of DEET alone sent the insects into a food frenzy. Now, 60 percent of mosquitoes exposed to DEET showed the BAR. In comparison, just 17 percent of bugs that hadn’t gone through the training procedure showed biting responses. When DEET Stops Working To see whether DEET-fan mosquitoes would change their responses to repellent-soaked humans, the team offered them a choice between two hands. One was covered in DEET, while the other wasn’t. While 100 percent of the untrained insects steered clear of the DEET hand, more than half of the trained insects opted for a meal of blood and insect repellent. The association wasn’t specific to human blood. A separate experiment trained the mosquitoes to link DEET to a sugar reward. The results were identical: Trained mosquitoes performed BAR in the presence of DEET. The results could be instructive outside the lab. People who want to avoid being bitten should be careful about how they apply DEET, said Lazzari. “If a mosquito bites someone who applied DEET to their skin several hours earlier and the concentration of the repellent is too low to repel the mosquito, but still strong enough for the insect to smell it, the mosquito may be more likely to bite people who smell of DEET.” Reference Lazzari CR, et al. Associative learning switches DEET valence from aversive to appetitive in Aedes aegypti . J Exp Biol . 2026;229:jeb251935. In fact, you would be hard pressed to find a sample of human blood, tissue or breast milk without detectable levels of at least one type of PFAS. 1,2 Making matters worse, researchers are continually uncovering links between human exposure to PFAS and poor health outcomes, including a weakened immune system, a heightened risk of kidney and testicular cancer, and pregnancy complications, including preeclampsia and reduced birth weight. 3,4 The levels of some PFAS considered safe in US drinking water are decreasing. 5 Despite this, The Trump administration is in the process of revoking and possibly rewriting proposed regulations for all but PFOA and PFOS, two of the most commonly used PFAS until the early 2000s. US maximum contaminant level goals for PFOA and PFOS are 0 parts per trillion – meaning there are no levels the US Environmental Protection Agency considers safe. Meanwhile, thousands of PFAS have not been studied and have no regulation or oversight. 6 In many cases, there is no monitoring data on their presence in consumer products, water and food. As an expert in chemical pollution , I have studied a wide range of synthetic and natural chemicals that can have harmful health effects for humans and wildlife. A major focus of my current research is tracing PFAS from their initial source – including consumer products, contaminated food and water, and the air – to their resulting fingerprint in an organism’s blood and tissues. 7 Continue reading below... First, though, we need to understand how these complex chemical mixtures are transformed as they accumulate in the body. What Are PFAS? PFAS are a large class of organic chemicals – meaning molecules that contain carbon atoms – that have fluorine atoms added to them. This fluorination allows PFAS to aggregate on surfaces in ways that are desirable for many applications. For example, PFAS are used in nonstick cookware, food packaging, cosmetics, textiles and even toilet paper, among many other commercial and industrial products. 8 They’re also heavily used in semiconductor manufacturing and lithium-ion batteries. 9 When PFAS are everywhere, they’re hard to avoid. PFAS are commonly called forever chemicals because of their astonishing persistence – due to the strong chemical bonds between carbon and fluorine, they don’t break down easily. This durability is desirable for manufacturers, as materials made with PFAS can function for a long time without degrading. However, persistence becomes problematic when PFAS leach or evaporate out of products and into the surrounding environment. PFAS can remain in drinking water sources and in sediment for decades to centuries. 10,11 If dissolved in water or released into the air, PFAS can also travel long distances from their point of origin, ending up in remote locations. 12 For example, PFAS initially released from industrial regions can end up in the blood of white sharks in the Atlantic Ocean or in Arctic environments. 13,14 PFAS Fingerprints What happens when PFAS are absorbed and accumulate in the body? When someone is exposed to PFAS, it leaves a unique pattern of chemical contamination – what researchers call a PFAS fingerprint – in their blood. 15 Studying these PFAS fingerprints enables scientists to learn about sources of PFAS exposure and how they differ among people who live in different places, have different jobs and use different products, among other factors. But to be able to use these PFAS fingerprints, researchers first need to understand how specific exposures contribute to someone’s PFAS fingerprint over time. The composition of this fingerprint is different from the mixture of chemicals someone was initially exposed to, as some PFAS accumulate in blood to a greater extent than others. Without understanding how a PFAS mixture is distorted and changed in the body, it’s very difficult to know what sources were major contributors to a person’s lifelong PFAS exposure. For example, firefighters and military service members use aqueous film-forming foams that contain hundreds of poorly studied PFAS. These are soapy, sudsy materials that form a film over fire and starve it of oxygen. They’re commonly used in emergencies, such as airplane crashes, train wrecks, vehicle fires or any other fire involving fuels. The PFAS in firefighting foam are suspected to be significant occupational health hazards. Jim Peaco/Yellowstone Digital Slide Files Many firefighters and first responders who have used these foams are now grappling with serious health problems, including cancer, and many have wondered whether PFAS contributed to their illness. A clearer understanding of the PFAS fingerprint that would be expected in someone’s blood after years of using these foams could help determine whether they are a unique source of the PFAS accumulating in their blood. PFAS in the Body Fingerprints at the scene of a crime are often a major clue leading detectives to the perpetrator. When it comes to identifying sources of PFAS contaminating human bodies, however, researchers like me aren’t always so lucky. For one, PFAS are typically present at low concentrations in the environment but can build up to higher levels in the body . For example, people drinking water containing PFOS will typically have levels 50 to 100 times higher in their blood than were measured in the water. 16 This is because the body’s rate of PFOS uptake exceeds its rate of excretion. But not all PFAS will increase in blood to the same degree. PFAS that are more likely to bind to biological components, such as proteins and fats, will more readily accumulate in the body. 17 As the mixture of chemicals in drinking water, for example, continues to accumulate in the body, these types of more bioaccumulative PFAS, such as PFOS, will make up a higher proportion of the fingerprint than other types. This distortion complicates my and other scientists’ job, since we need to be able to predict how much each PFAS accumulates in the body to estimate how these chemicals will change in the body. Do you know how much and what types of PFAS are in your water? show999/iStock via Getty Images Plus On top of predicting which PFAS will accumulate in the body and which will be excreted, researchers also have to contend with a person’s metabolism, the process by which chemicals – including some PFAS – are biologically transformed by the body. Although the chemical structure of PFAS may change in the body, the resulting chemical is usually still a PFAS: a highly fluorinated molecule. After entering the body, many types of PFAS used in different products can be transformed over days to years, while the highly fluorinated backbone of the molecule remains intact. By these processes, many different PFAS eventually transform into just a few highly persistent PFAS. 18 For example, many distinct PFAS containing a PFOS backbone can ultimately change to PFOS in the body. 19 Once these distinct PFAS have all become the same common chemical, it may be impossible to identify how a person was initially exposed. Studying real products that contain complex PFAS mixtures can help researchers get closer to finding biomarkers that can pinpoint a PFAS source in a person’s blood. The most effective way to protect human health would be to cease the use of PFAS entirely in all but the most essential of products. 20 Until then, consumers can look to resources such as those from the Green Science Policy Institute and Environmental Working Group to help them avoid PFAS in products they use. There are also a number of commercial laboratories that offer drinking water and blood testing for some common PFAS. But it’s important to remember that these tests don’t capture the whole picture of your PFAS fingerprint. 21 Scientists like me are still hard at work capturing many more PFAS that have been overlooked.
